howBattery_1: The battery is a short-term reserve for hard running. Running faster than about 15 km/h uses it up, and the faster the run, the quicker it goes. Below that pace it refills, fastest at a walk.
howBattery_2: We can't measure how tired or how fit a player actually is, so the battery shows what the same running would leave a typical professional. We run it for 200 typical professionals of different fitness and show the middle value.
howChartTitle: {name}: speed and the battery a typical pro would have
howChartSub: The opening clip's run and the eight minutes after it. Shaded: the seconds above 15 km/h. The typical pro's battery falls in those seconds and mostly refills in the rest.
howChartBattery: Battery a typical pro would have, %
howAgentsTitle: The commentary: written by AI, checked before it is shown
howAgents_1: Our code does the measuring and four AI agents write the words. Every number they get comes with its unit and the measurement it came from.
howAgentStep_1: Tracking of every player and the ball
howAgentStep_2: Our code measures the running and the battery
howAgentStep_3: Tools that hand the agents the numbers
howAgentStep_5: Agent 2 writes each line from published findings
howAgentStep_6: Agent 3 adapts it for fans or analysts
howAgentStep_7: Agent 4 checks it and blocks what the numbers don't support
howAgents_2: The check has two stages. Fixed rules come first and give the same answer every time: each number has to match the measurement, and each claim has to match published research. A second AI then reads the sentence and can block it but can't rewrite it. We tested the check on 192 sentences we wrote.
howAgents_3: The second AI can give different answers on different runs. The fixed rules always give the same one.
howDataTitle: What it needs from a real match
howData_1: Tracking data: the position of every player and the ball, 10 times a second, from cameras in the stadium or from the broadcast.
howData_3: Whether the ball is in play and who has it, and match events (passes, turnovers, shots) for some of the moments.
howData_4: Nothing worn by the players: no sensors, GPS vests or fitness tests.
howDataSynthetic: The matches on this site come from our own simulator, built on published sports science. Because we generate them, we know each player's true state and can test the battery against it. The simulated movement is checked against real tracking (IDSSE, SkillCorner, Metrica) and Premier League event data from Wyscout.
howLiveTitle: During a live match (not built yet)
howLiveIntro: The site replays recorded matches. The same steps could run during a game, but we haven't built or tested that.
howLive_1: Positions arrive from the stadium 10 times a second.
howLive_2: The replay smooths the positions using the moments before and after each one. Live, only the moments before are available, so speeds arrive slightly later.
howLive_3: The battery only uses the running so far, so it can update every second.
howLive_4: Each moment is detected once it is complete, for example when a player's hardest few minutes end.
howLive_5: Writing and checking a line takes the AI some time, so lines appear shortly after their moment.
howLive_6: Batteries and lines go to the broadcast as they are ready. We planned Azure Event Hubs for this and cut it to finish in time.
howMore: Formulas, tests and the research behind each number:
howBatteryTech: The model: a D′ balance (critical speed 4.1 ± 0.3 m/s, D′ 180 ± 54 m, from published tests), 200 draws and their weighted median. Analysts also see the 10 to 90% band for a typical pro.
howAgentsTech: Built with Microsoft Foundry and Agent Framework (gpt-5-mini), an MCP server with seven read-only tools, and the Verifier (rules, then an LLM pass that can only block).
howVer_1: Of 119 sentences that should have been blocked, the fixed rules blocked 87. With the AI check added, 116 were blocked.
howVer_2: Of 73 correct sentences, the fixed rules blocked none. With the AI check added, 1 was blocked by mistake.
